name: Direct lunar transfer
blurb: A five-day trip similar to Lunar Prospector’s. A faster arrival requires a larger braking burn.
notes: Lunar Prospector entered lunar orbit 105 hours after launch. The five-day duration rounds that example. The 2028 date, window, C3, arrival speed and maneuver allowance are scenario assumptions.

name: Low-energy lunar transfer
blurb: A looping route modeled on GRAIL. Spend months in cruise to arrive more gently and save braking propellant.
notes: GRAIL launched in September 2011 and entered lunar orbit around the turn of the year using a low-energy route. This explains the trade-off. The 2028 date and maneuver and arrival parameters are scenario assumptions.

name: Mars transfer — late 2028
blurb: A late-2028 launch with lower launch energy and a slower arrival than the late-2030 option. Cruise takes about ten months.
notes: Verified: the lowest-total-ΔV trajectory of the 2028 window (Traj_ID 20632): launch 2028-11-29, arrival 2029-09-29, 304 days, injection C3 8.2 km²/s², arrival burn 0.854 km/s at 250 km altitude. NASA Ames Trajectory Browser (one-way rendezvous, minimise total ΔV, all trajectories), retrieved 2026-11-15; raw answers in data/raw/trajbrowser/windows.json, re-run with scripts/data/fetch-trajbrowser.ts. Arrival v∞ is derived from the site's arrival burn, which it defines as slowing to escape speed at the listed radius: v∞² = (v_esc + Δv)² − v_esc². Game values: launchWindowDays and the tcmDvMs allowance. Estimates: min/max Sun distance.

name: Mars transfer — late 2030
blurb: The next window, two years later, arriving in 2031. It needs more launch energy and arrives faster, so braking costs more fuel.
notes: Verified: the lowest-total-ΔV trajectory of the 2030–31 window (Traj_ID 20662): launch 2030-12-21, arrival 2031-10-05, 288 days, injection C3 10.2 km²/s², arrival burn 1.107 km/s at 250 km altitude. name: Direct to Jupiter
blurb: Straight there in under 3 years — but it takes enormous launch energy, so your spacecraft must be light.
notes: Verified: the lowest-total-ΔV direct trajectory of the 2028–29 window (Traj_ID 515): launch 2028-12-31, arrival 2031-11-22, 1,056 days, injection C3 77.5 km²/s², arrival burn 0.220 km/s 1,000 km above the cloud tops. NASA Ames Trajectory Browser (one-way rendezvous, minimise total ΔV, all trajectories), retrieved 2026-11-15; raw answers in data/raw/trajbrowser/windows.json, re-run with scripts/data/fetch-trajbrowser.ts. (Jupiter needs the search limits raised to 6 years and 10 km/s.) Arrival v∞ is derived from the site's arrival burn, which it defines as slowing to escape speed at the listed radius: v∞² = (v_esc + Δv)² − v_esc². Game values: launchWindowDays and the tcmDvMs allowance. Estimates: min/max Sun distance.

name: Earth gravity assist (ΔV-EGA)
blurb: Launch gently, loop around the Sun, burn once in deep space, then slingshot past Earth to Jupiter. A third of the launch energy, 19 extra months.
notes: Verified: the lowest-total-ΔV Earth-flyby trajectory launching in 2029 (Traj_ID 1327): launch 2029-01-16, deep-space manoeuvre 611 m/s on day 383 plus 7 m/s at the flyby, Earth flyby on day 784, arrival 2033-07-06 after 1,632 days, injection C3 26.5 km²/s², arrival burn 0.269 km/s 1,000 km above the cloud tops. NASA Ames Trajectory Browser (one-way rendezvous, minimise total ΔV, all trajectories), retrieved 2026-11-15; raw answers in data/raw/trajbrowser/windows.json, re-run with scripts/data/fetch-trajbrowser.ts. (Jupiter needs the search limits raised to 6 years and 10 km/s.) Arrival v∞ is derived from the site's arrival burn, which it defines as slowing to escape speed at the listed radius: v∞² = (v_esc + Δv)² − v_esc². Juno flew the same kind of path: launch 2011-08-05, Earth flyby 2013-10-09, arrival 2016-07-05 UTC (NSSDCA 2011-040A). Game values: launchWindowDays and the tcmDvMs allowance. Estimates: min/max Sun distance.
